utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger, today -- I said yesterday that we would hear you first thing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before I begin with the issue raised by the Chamber at the end of the session yesterday, I might mention the resolution of the scheduling issue which was also on our agenda. This is -- we did discuss the matter with the Defence. This was an impressive example, actually, of both sides doing their utmost to compromise and offering concessions in their previous positions to accommodate the other. In this case, we made the last accommodation and urged them to go through the door first. So we'll be moving forward on the schedule that Mr. Robinson proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. The Chamber appreciates the parties' co-operation very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I mentioned to Mr. Robinson this morning in -- also that I would at the same time note another issue that's been on the table which, unfortunately, has not resolved it in the same level of progress and that's the issue of the failure to comply with 65 ter and the absence of adequate factual summaries and/or statements. We took certain steps toward resolving that, but those turned out to be utterly ineffectual, that is, we -- I won't go into the details, but the anticipated first step toward resolving it that the Prosecution expected to receive from the Defence did not turn out to be an effective measure in any way. So that issue is still very much on the table. We are going to address it with greater intensity during the break, if we can, but that may be something we'll be bringing to the attention of the Trial Chamber and I wanted to alert the Trial Chamber to that possibility. That said, Mr. President, I wanted to speak on the issue that you asked me to address and that is the time spent by the Prosecution in cross-examination. By way of background, I note that you indicated, among other things, that the Prosecution had used much more time in cross-examination than the Defence used in examination and re-examination, that the evidence presented by these witnesses was limited, with short statements, very few associated exhibits and - as mentioned - often a limited number of issues. I hope I won't spend too much time telling you why the Prosecution is not taking too much time, but given the amount of time available between last night and this morning, this may be a case of it takes more time to prepare a short letter than a longer one, but I'll do my best. I'd like to note preliminarily that there is no gap, no friction, no conflict between the Court's interest in the most efficient possible cross-examinations and therefore the most efficient possible trial and the Prosecution's interest in exactly the same thing. We want to move forward as expeditiously as we can while remaining true to the mandate to maintain a trial that pursues the ascertainment of the truth and the achievement of justice. And we feel that actually given our extensive knowledge of the case, we are in the best possible position to assess the balance between the issues needed to be raised in cross-examination and those extremely significant responsibilities. And as we've progressed, we've attempted to identify areas where such efficiencies can take place. The Court will have noted the recurring themes that seem to arise in statement after statement. We consider that to the extent we have effectively dealt with those with certain witnesses, that to the extent those tend to arise with similarly situated witnesses, we do not need to spend as much time or indeed, perhaps, any time addressing those same issues which have been thrashed out and clarified with previous witnesses. And we also constantly meet to identify basically the state of play with respect to the kinds of issues that are raised by witnesses, all in the interest of making the examinations as short and effective as they can possibly be. And I would emphasize that a great deal of out-of-court time, an enormous amount of out-of-court time goes into just that effort. But I wanted to actually turn to the Court's specific points about the balance between the length of the statements, the amount of time taken in direct examination and re-examination, and the time taken by the Prosecution for cross-examination. And I hope I can shed some light on factors that may not have been immediately apparent. Frankly, it -- while it may be correct that the statements comprise fewer pages than statements, for example, submitted by the Prosecution during the course of its case, it is simply not the case that there is any necessary relationship between the issues -- the significance and number of issues raised and the number of pages that a statement comprises, nor is there any relationship between the number of pages and the difficulty, complexity, or necessary length of a cross-examination, and let me explain. With respect to the format, that is, that there's no necessary relationship between the length of a statement and the number of issues raised or the need for time spent in cross-examination, the reductio ad absurdum of that is frankly something I've mentioned to students, for example, in the course of discussions about this very issue in making that very point, and that's a situation where to make the point you would say: Look, what if somebody comes in and says, I was with the accused the entire length of the war or the entire length of the -- and take a domestic case of the events at issue months and months and years and years, and that person committed no crime. You now have ten seconds to cross-examine. Now, that sounds absurd, but in a sense that's the situation we are facing here. We have commander after commander after commander coming in with sweeping statements about what happened along the lines of: We always complied with IHL, we never fired into the depth, we only received orders to obey international humanitarian law, we never fired at civilians. Now, those issues cover basically the entirety of the Prosecution case and compel cross-examination. So they put virtually everything on the table. The Prosecution has no recourse but to address those things. Now, the paradox is that by doing it in that way, not only do those statements require us to cover a vast array of issues, but they make it more difficult to do so because it's incumbent then upon the Prosecution to identify the underlying factors that allow for a meaningful cross-examination that are not covered in a statement. So it's vastly easier when much of the background work has been done by a detailed statement that lets you know who, what, where, and how so you can really get to the crux of the issue rather than having to reconstruct it during the course of the cross-examination. Just as a -- the same thing is true, for example, of associated exhibits. The number of associated exhibits, whether -- the fact that there are few associated exhibits doesn't necessarily mean there's less -- there's less time needed for cross-examination. It can be just the opposite, and one example that comes to mind is the very first cross-examination. The Court may recall that a large number of additional paragraphs and quite a significant volume, dozens and dozens of additional exhibits were added at the last minute to the statement. Now, that did not expand the estimated time for cross-examination. Indeed, the Prosecution took significantly less time than it had originally estimated, and part of the reason was that those additional exhibits gave us access to information that allowed us to effectively cross-examine the witness directly. So, for example, we were able to expose the mis-characterisation of the Vrbanja bridge incident on the basis of a document that was an associated exhibit that indicated that contemporaneously the witness was aware that what had been said in -- what he was now saying in the statement was not true. So that's one example of the seemingly paradoxical relationship between the length of the -- the length of a statement and the length of cross-examination and the fact that it's important to reject the idea that a short statement necessarily means a short cross. It's not the case at all, as I noted. Now, I mentioned earlier the -- what I consider to be the extraordinary efforts behind the scenes that the Prosecution makes to identify relevant documents, relevant issues, that should be brought to the Court's attention to illuminate the issues and simultaneously determine which of the issues raised in the statement need to be raised. And I need to emphasize that this was -- this has not been the case where the Prosecution has simply reflexively marched through the statement, addressing issue after issue raised by the Defence in those statements. I didn't have time to canvass the team generally or cover the cross-examinations in their entirety, but a simple quick review indicated that there were large amounts - many, many paragraphs of many, many statements - that we simply discarded because either the focus was on the general credibility of the witness or because we considered them sufficiently peripheral or marginal that they should not consume the time of the Court. And all of that is reflected in the stats that I've been able to gather about the cross-examinations and the time we've had. So here, for example, I have the statistics for the estimated times for cross-examination and the times that the Prosecution has taken. I think it's a very impressive table. We've come in under, as the Court mentioned a few days ago, asking us to be alert to the fact that we were being more efficient in cross-examination than we had appreciated and to try to make those estimates conform a little more closely to where we ended up, but they're modest -- relatively modest estimates and they are very, very impressive results based on those cross-examinations. I also want to mention, by the way, that there was never an instance where a reduced time for cross-examination, that is, the difference between the estimate and the time we actually took threatened that there would not be a witness here because we were in contact with the Defence and Mr. Robinson throughout. So they were always aware of the most contemporary and most current estimate. A similar statistic, Mr. President, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just staying there. What number do you have in -- the estimate versus actual time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have that percentage. What I have is -- I was just looking down the individual -- and I can read some of them and the majority come in as -- I mean, I can read them off one at a time, it's a bit anecdotal, but I was highlighting the ones that were -- so I look at the first one, the first estimate was 5.5, it came in at under 3 and a half. The second one was 4, it came in at under an hour. The third one was 4.5, it came in under 3 hours, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In total I think the actual time is about 57 per cent of your estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And really, Mr. President, that is not because we've inflated the estimates. It's because we've been constantly working to identify what really needs to be done and, as you would expect and as I kind of alluded to at the beginning of my discussion, the more you work on something the more you're in a position to make it more efficient and that's what's been happening. A similar example of the efficiency of the Prosecution, I believe, can be found in the percentages of time used by the parties. And what I can tell the Court is that based on our statistics, it appears that the Prosecution is -- that the same percentages of time are being used by the parties as during the Prosecution case. And why is that significant? It's significant because, as you can see, the Defence is using scarcely any time in its tendering of the 92 ter submissions. And that would mean if the Prosecution was maintaining the same level of efficiency in cross-examination, that is, was taking -- consuming the same amount in cross-examination that the Defence had used, that our percentage of time taken in the course of this case would obviously increase; that is, now the Defence takes no time in tendering the statements. Obviously then the time taken for cross-examination would consume a much greater percentage of the overall allotment. But that's not the case. These percentages have remained the same and they've remained the same because the Prosecution has tried just as hard to keep these examinations as efficient as possible. Now, I tried to promise at the beginning that I wouldn't take more time than necessary and perhaps I've overstayed my welcome in that respect, but I want to emphasize two things. And that is that the Prosecution is willing at all times to take on further guidance about where Prosecution -- where examinations can be conducted more efficiently and we will certainly take those suggestions on board. But I think it's important to emphasize that the role of the Prosecution in cross-examination is central to the identification of the evidence necessary for this Trial Chamber to make the significant decisions it has to make. Nothing, in our submission, that the Prosecution has done thus far would suggest or, much less, warrant the imposition of time-limits. We think quite the contrary. And we think to do so would jeopardise potentially our ability to get you the information that you need and deserve. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one -- with respect to the ratio referred to, to the effect that the ratio during the Defence case so far is similar to that during the Prosecution case, did you not from time to time or oftentimes that the time spent by the Defence was unreasonably too lengthy?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One thing I wanted to -- you know, I noted that one thing in the course of -- in the effort to be as quick as possible, one thing I didn't mention that I wanted to mention earlier and that is I did say that the Prosecution has attempted to be as efficient as possible. I wanted to explicitly mention that among the things the Prosecution has avoided is dealing with topics not raised by the statement, dealing with peripheral topics, trying to address every statement, unnecessary arguments the witness -- and I could go on, basically avoided all those factors that prompted the Prosecution during the course of the -- of its case and during the course of Defence examinations to note that time might not be used as efficiently as possible. And I think for the most part, by the way, we - with the exception of the very beginning of the case when those issues tended to be raised - I think we largely refrained from assessments of how much time should be allotted to the Defence, if any, and how it should be handled directly in favour of simply identifying at any given moment whether a relevant issue was being addressed or whether the accused was needlessly pursuing an issue that was not productive. So I certainly would -- I'm not going to dispute the fact that we didn't disagree with the Trial Chamber's assessment that the accused's cross-examinations were not as efficient as possible and very, very often - if not almost uniformly - ventured into unnecessary areas in unproductive ways. So I -- you're right, I don't want to compare those -- to make a comparison between our obligations to be as efficient as possible and what the accused did. But I think my point was that given -- given the fact that the Trial Chamber did impose limits and tried to keep it within a reasonable period of time, the fact that we are maintaining the same percentage now is a testimonial to our efforts to keep those cross-examinations as efficient as possible. I'd also mention - I think it needs to be said because I think it's fair - I think the Court was careful at all times, insofar as I recall, to make it clear to the accused that to the extent he can -- he was dealing with issues fairly and efficiently, the Court would not constrain him. And I think the Court emphasized that time and again, and I -- for all the reasons that I've explained, I submit that the Prosecution is dealing with these cross-examinations as efficiently as it possibly can and will continue to do so and refine the efficiency even further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to respond to Mr. Tieger. I can only say that based on their difficulties, it would be easier to perceive what difficulties the Defence encounters given their limited resources. I would like to apologise to the Trial Chamber and especially Judge Morrison for interrupting his question the day before yesterday; however, with all due respect for the efforts of the interpreters, neither I nor the witness received that as the interpretation of a question but rather as a statement. Some other interventions of mine arise from that. I'm concerned because of the -- because of mistakes in the interpretation. Sometimes even erroneous statements in the Prosecutor's questions which may influence the course of the examination. My interventions during additional questions may be belated when we're talking about misquotations or misinterpretations. I beg your indulgence, please allow me to intervene with corrections in the transcript or corrections when questions contain misquotations. And once again, I would like to apologise to His Excellency Judge Morrison for having interrupted his intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's very kind, Dr. Karadzic, but I don't think an apology is actually necessary. I certainly didn't perceive that one was necessary. For myself, if the transcript is not accurate then it -- it assists everybody if there is an intervention to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I reiterate here now again that it's imperative on your part to advise the witnesses from the region to speak slow, given that they -- the situation regarding the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, if I could make one quick --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- sorry, just one quick point about the interpretation and maybe it stands -- it's a bit obvious, but everyone would have to share Judge Morrison's observation. However, one thing we have noted and that occurred yesterday when the interpreter said -- following an intervention: Well, that's the same thing. In other words, it's another way of saying the same thing. So there are many ways or there are often situations where there are synonyms that are basically identical. If we're going to have interventions that identify such synonyms because Mr. Karadzic thinks that he would have chosen a different one, that will be rather cumbersome. So I think he's going to need to distinguish between genuine problems and circumstances that don't change the meaning of what was translated in a meaningful way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Tieger. We'll consider your submission. Shall we bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Malinovic. If you could take a seat. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Malinovic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please feel relaxed. Things proceed very smoothly here. I have to remind myself of something and I have to tell you that we should make brief pauses between questions and answers for the sake of the interpreters. I would also like to ask you to speak slowly so that everything can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D6233, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give the Defence team a statement and is this the statement that you can see before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement reflect everything that you had to say?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is everything that you stated correctly recorded and were you able to verify it and read through your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Everything was accurately recorded, I checked that. I read through my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you here today viva voce, would your answers be the same in substance?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I tender this packet into evidence pursuant to 92 ter, Rule 92 ter? I believe we have five associated documents and this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, before I hear from the Prosecution, I'm not sure whether those documents are relevant or necessary for the purpose of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Well, they corroborate a portion of her statement, but I'll leave it to you as to whether you think that needs to be corroborated or not. And in the event you do admit them, I would ask that two of them that were not on our 65 ter list be allowed to be added, and that's the first one, 15020 and 15024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm of the view that we can do without them. We'll admit the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I will now read out a summary of Mrs. Malinovic's statement in English. [In English] Zeljka Malinovic is a medical technician by profession. She worked at the Novi Grad - Otoka clinic until May the 2nd, 1992. The medical staff was ethnically mixed but intra-ethnic relations among the staff had already begun to deteriorate from the autumn 1991. The establishment of the multi-party system in the territory of BH led to the first intra-ethnic disputes in the town of Sarajevo. At their rallies in the town and surrounding area, the Muslims and Croats glorified the struggle for the secessionist forces in Croatia and erected an open front toward the Serbs, who began to feel afraid and anxious about their like and coexistence in the territory in BH. Because of these tensions, barricades sprung up on all major roads in the early spring of 1992. Muslims and Serbs set up the barricades in the areas where they were a majority, while Croats were mostly on the barricades together with the Muslims. At the beginning of March 1992, most barricades on the roads were removed but groups of armed Muslim civilians remained at all important junctions, checking day and night the papers of the civilians passing through their controls. These were members of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. Once they had established, by looking at the identity cards, that someone was Serb, they would conduct the check in a cynical and humiliating manner. These Muslim paramilitary formations also made lists for parts of the town and the apartment buildings where Serbs lived and searched them under the pretense of looking for radio transmitter sets and weapons. In addition to this, they would also forcibly take into custody and lead away Serbian civilians. Those taken into custody would be held for hours, interrogated, threatened, and maltreated, all this usually conducted in improvised areas such as entrances of buildings and business premises. Her father was detained twice. In mid-April 1992, three members of the Green Berets searched her apartment, conducting themselves in a rough manner and threatening to kill her and her family. Feared for their lives and considered the possibility of fleeing to a Serb majority area until the situation stabilised. Whenever Serbs put complaints to the MUP, police, in Sarajevo about these issues concerning the Muslim paramilitaries, they would be harassed and maltreated even more and often also labelled as sniper shooters, regardless of whether they were males or females. They would be taken to improvised prisons from where they hardly ever returned. This evidences the complicity between the legal forces of the MUP and illegal paramilitary formations. In late April 1992, Slavisa Kravljaca was taken away and tortured by members of the Green Berets by having nails hammered under his fingernails. After that, they took Kravljaca to Zavnobih Square where a crowd of Muslim men and women stoned him. Alongside the medical staff, there would be ten Green Berets members armed with automatic rifles. In the afternoon they would fire in bursts through the clinic's windows in the direction of the Viktor Bubanj barracks where a JNA unit was billeted. They also swore at the Serbs and announced that they would soon raze the Serb settlement of Nedzarici to the ground, and sow wheat where the Serb houses stood. That day she decided she would not go back to work and she and her mother left to Nedzarici. Her father, Uros, and her brother remained in the flat, an area which like the broader Alipasino Polje area was controlled by Juka Prazina, a renowned pre-war criminal whose soldiers were mostly people from criminal circles. Juka Prazina's unit was supported by parts of the so-called Laste Special Unit. Zeljka Malinovic met many exchanged Serb girls and women who had been raped by Muslim forces. They were only exchanged once they had reached their seventh or eighth month of pregnancy and could no longer have an abortion. After the formation of the VRS on the 12th of May, 1992, she joined the army as a volunteer and was assigned to the medical battalion in Nedzarici, where she stayed until 5th of May, 1993. Her unit engaged exclusively in defensive operations aimed to protect all civilians in its rear. They intervened daily taking care of wounded and killed Serbs, more than 350 persons in one year, the majority of which were civilians. Most wounds were to the head and the upper body due to the sniper fire by Muslim soldiers. Others were caused by random actions of the Muslim artillery against Nedzarici. Serbian forces in -- on the Nedzarici front were in an inferior position vis-a-vis Muslim forces, positioned at higher buildings. Nedzarici was completely encircled by Muslim forces. The only road her unit has -- had was the Kasindolska Street, Ilidza, along which it was only possible to move at night due to Muslim fire. Muslim forces also cut off the supply of electricity and water to the part of Nedzarici under Serbian control. Muslim forces fired at her unit's ambulance whenever they had the opportunity, regardless it was marked with the red cross in line with the regulations. In her year of service, out of 11 members of her unit eight were wounded during interventions. UNPROFOR members witnessed some of these incidents and had to intervene at least on one occasion to protect the ambulance. Muslim forces also systematically violated truce agreements, while claiming in the media that violations had been on the Serb side. This usually happened when either international forces or foreign journalists were on the line. Exchanged Serbs from Sarajevo were starved and physically maltreated by members of the Muslim formations. After every attack casualties would also be exchanged. Serbs exchanged the bodies of killed Muslim soldiers while Muslims would return bodies of Serbian civilians. With regard to Zeljka Malinovic's father, Uros Rakanovic, he was arrested on 31st of May, 1992, by the Green Berets, interrogated, and physically maltreated. On 2nd of June, 1992, he was arrested again and beaten up during interrogations, the result of which was both legs and most of his ribs broken. The following day he was taken to the front line to call out to Zeljka Malinovic and her brother to surrender. After this he was taken to the central prison in Sarajevo where he spent 24 days until his transfer to Viktor Bubanj prison, where he died on 11th of November, 1992. On 28 of September, 2006, on the basis of DNA analysis her father's remains were identified and recovered in the Lav cemetery, lion's cemetery, in Sarajevo. The autopsy established that all his ribs and both legs were broken and the lower jaw was missing. [Interpretation] I don't have any questions for Mrs. Malinovic at this point in time. What I have just read out is the summary. I'm waiting for the interpretation. I do apologise. This was the summary and I would like to tender this statement into evidence. And if the exhibits are of any help to the Chamber, I would like to tender them too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We dealt with it. Any further questions, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at this point in time, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Iodice. If -- my apology if my pronunciation is not correct, but I forgot to ask when Mr. Karadzic tendered the 92 ter statement -- but I took it that there was no objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Malinovic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in this case in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be further cross-examined by the Prosecution. Yes, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Malinovic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you for meeting with me the day before yesterday. First I would like to ask you about the circumstances of your Defence statement. The day before yesterday you told me that you have been following the trial from the beginning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And that you volunteered to become a witness; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you gave your statement over the phone, more or less, six months ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: First I gave it in person. That's what I told Mr. Zoran Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: All right. And then you saw it written down for the first time in The Hague and that's when you signed it; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I met Mr. President, Mr. Marko gave it to me to sign and he provided me with the statement here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And when we met, you made a small correction to your statement. You said there is a mistake in paragraph 10 where it is written that the shooting at the Otoka clinic happened in the afternoon. You corrected that and said it was in the evening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it happened around 1900 hours, to be precise, so it was in the early evening and continued until late at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is a single incident that took place on the 1st of May, correct, between the night of the 1st of May to the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to comment on the interpretation. It says "one," but -- or it was said "one," but the interpretation was "the only." That is what the answer depends on. [In English] "The only," [Interpretation] It was translated as "one" in the Serbian language instead of "the only."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see much difference. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So now I would like to discuss the check-point in the searches that you discuss in paragraph 5 of your statement. You mentioned that each ethnicity set up barricades in the part of town where they were the majority. And so when in paragraph 7 you say that the movement of citizens was entirely controlled by the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, you are referring to the parts of town where Muslims were the majority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And when in paragraph 7 you say that the Muslim paramilitary formations made lists of Serb apartments to be searched, I take it that you've never seen these lists; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen the lists, but I heard about such things. I was told that they did such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now discuss the torture and stoning of Slavisa Kravljaca in Zavnobih Square. Did you personally know this man?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: No, my brother did.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you say that was a -- he was a civil servant. What exactly did he do? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: In your statement you said that Slavisa Kravljaca was a civil servant by profession.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Slavisa Kravljaca was a Serb from Nedzarici who went to have a coffee in the cafe that he would go to before the war. I didn't say that he was a statesman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's -- let us upload the statement -- I think it is in front of you. Do you have a hard copy with you, Ms. Malinovic? It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: If you look towards the end of paragraph 9, when you say: "In late April 1992 ..."

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is. Slavisa Kravljaca was taken in, he was maltreated, members of the Green Berets, and so on and so forth. So he was a civilian who went to have a coffee in the cafe that he would visit before the war. He was a 17-year-old young man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see your statement there, six lines from the bottom in para 9 it says: April 1992, Slavisa Kravljaca, and civil. It's translated "a civil servant." You said he was a civil servant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. And did you hear about Kravljaca having nails hammered under his fingernails from others or did you see his hands?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: A man who was my neighbour told me about this. He was a medical technician, as I was, because there was a clinic toward -- next to my building and they brought him there. He pulled the nails out of his fingers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something that is missing because the witness said this was something she was told by a man who personally took the nails out of his fingers.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Did you personally witness the actual stoning when it took place?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: I saw my neighbours who went there and they called on me to stone him. I remained in the stairwell of my building. When they returned they asked me why hadn't I gone there. One of them boasted about having looked for a large stone to hit him with so that it would hurt him as much as possible. But I didn't go there. I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So you didn't see it happening?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: -- couldn't watch that. No, I didn't, but I heard the noise. It was near my building. Do you understand me when I say "the noise" - that's the term we use - it means the screaming, the crying out, the noise, these ugly words, the racket.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Do you know if he survived?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally met him in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And did you ever report this event to -- during or after the war, including to the Serb authorities in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Which events? Are you referring to Slavisa Kravljaca? I can't answer because I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you report the stoning of Kravljaca to the Serb authorities at any point?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this. I had no need to make a statement. On a couple of occasions he appeared on our TV, so he described the event himself. So there was no need for me to go and confirm his statement anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the people who took part in it? You said they were your neighbours. Do you remember any names?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? I remember very few of my neighbours from my building. I'm seeking to forget because of my father. Those were women. Those were primarily women. Women were the main protagonists of that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And -- and do you -- the square where the incident took place was the square where you lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And it was surrounded by high-rise apartment buildings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: The square -- yes, yes. It is indeed surrounded by high-rise apartment buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And as you said, it was very noisy so many people would have seen or heard what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Malinovic, we -- so many people took part or, anyway, somehow heard or witnessed this incident, and yet in 20 years we never heard anything about it. We heard of many crimes. We heard of the shooting of the wedding guest in Bascarsija, and do you think that after 20 years such an horrific crime of a 17-year-old stoned in a public square would have not come to light at all?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what, it was heard about but on our television, on Serbian television. It was reported. I heard about it on several occasions. I heard Slavisa Kravljaca's statement on our television. What other things were heard, I don't know. I'm telling you the truth and I'm telling you about what I saw. And I know what that woman told me, that neighbour of mine who approached me, and two of my Croatian colleagues were present when that was happening. It was not just me who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move on to the incident that we already discussed during our meeting between the Green Berets at the Otoka clinic and the barracks of the JNA. In paragraph 10 you describe their arrival and the shooting that followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Can I call up 65 ter 24162.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Malinovic, the day before yesterday I showed you this map and you marked on it the location of the Otoka clinic where you worked with a circle and a C next to it, and then the bigger circle, the barracks, with a B next to it. Do you recognise it -- do you recognise the map?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you also put an arrow at the location from which the Green Berets were shooting, and that's the arrow that we see on the map; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We can see it, not very clearly, though, but yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And that's roughly -- and they were shooting roughly from the centre of the clinic, is that right? That's what, more or less, we see here?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately there. Not from the very centre of the clinic but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And when we talked the other day, you also told me that while the shooting was ongoing, you and your colleagues were hiding out of fear; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you could hear the shooting but you couldn't really see exactly what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? We were on the same floor from which fire was opened. Only a corridor separated us and some of them opened fire from there. We did hide among the archives, among the shelves with the patients' files, all of the patients' files. That's where we hid. A Muslim doctor reacted and asked them to stop firing because our lives were threatened. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And going back to the map, do you agree with me that the barracks are on a hill on the south bank of the river?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And the clinic is on the north side of the river and at the same level as the river?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, the Viktor Bubanj was not on a hilltop. It was an elevation, a sloping terrain. And our clinic was across the road from the Viktor Bubanj barracks, right across the road from there. And the distance was not that great because we could see everything with our naked eye from a window of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a look now at 65 ter 24101, which is the same photo that I already showed you. Do you see the barracks here?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please perhaps -- aha, now I can see that, yes. It was a bit small and kind of far away, but now I have spotted it. It's in the corner. Now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And maybe with the assistance of the usher could you mark the barracks.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is it. It's a bit blurred, but yes, I'm sure it is that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: If you could please mark it again because I think something went wrong.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see it now. And you also see the high-rise buildings between the barracks and the other bank of the river where the clinic is; right? And you're nodding. I take that's a "yes"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So if you could please put the date on the photo and your name. Today's the 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Could we have that admitted into evidence, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Let's now look at the barracks from a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 24100.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Do you see the barracks here?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Do you see the clinic here behind the buildings?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: It was 20 years ago. I can't really recognise it, but I think that it is in the left-hand side corner perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, may I add something to what I've already said? I believe that half the barracks is missing. This is not the entire barracks. Before the war, the barracks was a much bigger building. And there was a military prison there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That is, in fact, the same shape that we saw on the map; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so. But -- but, we can see the clinic and we can see how they could have opened fire on the Viktor Bubanj barracks, but what I see in the map, there is a parking-lot because as you see things now, they could not have opened fire on the Viktor Bubanj barracks because of the buildings. But I know I passed by the Viktor Bubanj barracks a hundred times and this is just one part of it. And believe me when I say that the rest is now a grassy patch. There's no barracks there, just grass.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Could I have this photo admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5994, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I want to move on now to your -- to your conclusion at the end of paragraph 10 where you talk about this incident. And you say: "This is one example of how the members of the Patriotic League and Green Berets used the medical facilities and the buildings in Sarajevo as their firing positions." You only witnessed this one incident at the Otoka clinic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I heard on their radio about the Lake Kosevo hospital. They talked about several occasions when JNA soldiers opened fire on medical institutions. When I returned in the morning -- I don't know if I'm speaking too fast. When I returned from my duty service the following morning, I switched on Sarajevo TV and I heard on the news that the JNA launched an attack on my clinic from the Viktor Bubanj barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now to your experience in Nedzarici. In your statement - and I'm referring to paragraphs 19 and 26 - you discuss various issues and say that the Muslim side always provoked the Serb side and your unit was only engaged in defence combat. Now, Nedzarici was quite small; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: You must have seen that Serbs had heavy weapons in Nedzarici; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a paramedic. I didn't know anything about the military. The only thing I know is that they brought wounded and dead people to my clinic. And that's all I know. I know nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That's right. You weren't involved in fighting. You weren't involved in the military. You weren't involved in any combat action; correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I worked in the clinic. I'm a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Malinovic, do you have a statement with you? Could you take a look at para 19.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out the first sentence aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I claim systematically that all truces were systematically violated by the Muslim side."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean, "all truces were systematically violated by the Muslim side," what do you know about that or what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was that while I was affiliated with the medical service, if I may be allowed to speak that way, those of us who were on duty on that day, we would have preferred not to have a truce because the biggest number of wounded and dead was during a truce, irrespective of the weather conditions. Come hell or high water, rain or shine, the biggest number of casualties were in truces. They opened fire from Dobrinja Pet, from Vojnicko [phoen] Polje, Mojmilo, from behind Alipasino Polje, from the Oslobodjenje building, from the student residential buildings. There is also a feature called Stupsko Brdo which we referred to as Betonara. In other words, we were surrounded by snipers. Even that passage towards Ilidza was under constant sniper fire from Butmir and that was just that one passage that we had in the direction of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Malinovic. Ms. Iodice, I take it you have more questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question and then one last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I just want to follow-up on what Judge Kwon asked you and you said you didn't see any heavy weapons. Mile Sladoje, who was the SRK commander of the Nedzarici barracks, gave a statement to the Defence - and that was 1D5647 and I'm referring to paragraphs 5 and 6 - and he stated that there were mortars and a tank in Nedzarici, but you didn't see those; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that man at all. I really don't know who you're talking about. I didn't even know what the names of the wounded were, let alone the fighters, the combatants.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And for the last question I would like to move very quickly to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, we passed the time to take a break, but, Mr. Karadzic, if you have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Only one, Excellency, only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P993 -- P5993. It is a photo that has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Malinovic, please, can you mark the clinic in this photo? Are there any new things here that didn't exist at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Could this photo be zoomed in a little? Can the photo please be zoomed in a little?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the central part be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the photo please be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this sufficient? Just wait till assisted --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that photo taken at the time or is this a photo of a new date, and how do you conclude that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: This is a photo of a new date. This was not taken before the war, before the breakout of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the current appearance of the Viktor Bubanj barracks and the court in Sarajevo. This is how things are at the moment. The Viktor Bubanj barracks was a military prison and it wasn't like this. The facade is different. This is now a photo depicting the court in Sarajevo. I really don't know what court that is. I know it's a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know the photo is of a newer date?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: The facade is new. I saw it in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about this mosque, is it an old mosque or a mosque that was built recently?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: This is a very new mosque. It didn't -- did not exist before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the map that you were shown, you don't know what that map depicts, what times?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Malinovic, for having come to testify here. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA MALINOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that concludes your evidence, Mrs. Malinovic. On behalf of the Chamber, I also would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We'll rise all together. We'll have a break for 20 minutes and resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although the blinds are drawn at the moment, we are in open session. Before we bring in the next witness I was about to raise this issue. Yes, I will do that. Although we admitted the previous witness's statement and let the evidence go, speaking for myself, I was struggling to understand the relevance of her testimony overall, whether it was not tu quoque at all. So do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I would like to -- I would like to respond, Your Excellency. [Interpretation] We were accused -- I and my army were accused for the fighting around and in Sarajevo. In the indictment Sarajevo has been described in one way, from one perspective, and I believe that it is essential to demonstrate what the situation was like on the other side of the confrontation line, what forced us, normal people, to defend our settlements for four years. It's not to justify this, but to show the reason for which we fought for four years. And also the issue is who was attacking. Light could be shed on this only by calling people who suffered those attacks and who responded to those attacks out of necessity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I will make it very simple. I'd like to reiterate two points. First, it is you, not the Serbian army or Serb people or anybody else, that was indicted in this case. So what matters is individual responsibility on your part. Second, who started the attack is not relevant for the purpose of this case at all. So I was concerned very much about delving into whether the nature of certain combat activities was defensive or offensive. It's all related jus ad bellum as I indicated yesterday. In the future, the Chamber will keep a closer look as to the relevance of the Defence witnesses' evidence and, if necessary, it may consider not allowing the evidence at all. But keep that in mind in the future.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just add something to my answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I understand the indictment, I haven't been accused for individual acts, but because of the joint criminal enterprise, participation or creation of that enterprise, that includes the conduct of my army in relation to Sarajevo. So it is essential to see what was happening on the other side, not in order to justify anything but, quite simply, because it's not a matter of individual responsibility. It is a matter of objective responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is not arguing with you. Just bear in mind what I said to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the curtains are drawn we don't need to go to closed -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness has protective measures of image distortion. In order to bring him in, we need to go to closed session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, lift the blinds, please. Good morning, sir. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I stand up? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Trifunovic, as you may be aware by now that the Chamber has granted the protective measures of image distortion for you, which means that while this trial is broadcast outside, the people outside the courtroom cannot see your face. You'll be viewed like this. Can you show him the image of his face which has been distorted. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D6250.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for that to come up, Mr. Trifunovic, did you give the Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation. I'd like to ask you to wait for the interpretation too and we should speak slowly so that the interpreters can interpret what we are saying accurately. Is that the statement that you can see before you on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read through the statement and can you confirm that it accurately reflects what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today viva voce in the courtroom, would the substance of your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this package pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit the statement as well as two associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Exhibit D2444 through D2446. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a summary of Mr. Trifunovic's statement in English. [In English] Miladin Trifunovic is a professional driver by occupation. During the war he held the rank of captain. After the multi-party elections, the situation in all parts of BH started changing and becoming more difficult. Joint ethnic guards were formed on the Serb initiative before the war in Vogosca to guard housing and other facilities. This lasted until groups of the Muslims and Croats started appearing in the streets carrying linked flags. To protect themselves Serbs also started closing ranks, especially since it was common knowledge that the Muslims were arming themselves on a massive scale and forming paramilitary units. The Patriotic League was formed in Vogosca in mid-June 1991. In April 1992, after the war had already begun, the Serbian municipality was formed in Vogosca. From March 1992 onwards, with more intensity than ever before, they could hear bursts of small arms fire coming from the Muslim-majority settlements. In his statement, Miladin Trifunovic recalls a series of incidents where several civilians were tortured, burnt, killed, and beheaded. On 17th through 18th April 1992, following several previous attempts, Muslim forces raided the Pretis factory, although Serbs managed to regain control over the area. Groups of armed citizens were formed as part of the Vogosca Territorial Defence. On April 18th, 1992, after Muslim paramilitary units had carried out several armed operations, the Territorial Defence was mobilised and the Vogosca Light Infantry Territorial Brigade was formed. He was appointed commander since no professional personnel could be found. The main road linking Vogosca and other Serbian municipalities passed through the Pretis factory. Throughout the entire war, over 1 and a half kilometres of the road were under permanent sniper fire and many pedestrians, civilians and passengers in motor vehicles were killed on these stretches. On June 8, 1992, Muslim forces mounted a ferocious attack from the direction of Sarajevo, pushing back Serb forces from Zuc, after which the zone of responsibility did not change until the end of the war. As a result, at this segment of their defence, the balance of power favoured the Muslims many times over. It should be stressed that Zuc was a dominant point on his unit's entire defence line on that axis. The brigade was manned exclusively by local population. They had enormous problems with logistics support and difficulties in the supply -- supplied of fuel, artillery rounds, and medical materials. For food and washing the soldiers relied on their own households, for which the defence had been organised in the first place. The opposing forces were those of the 1st Corps of BH army. Neither his brigade of any of the -- or any of the neighbouring ones were ever carried any offensive activities. He was never aware of the idea that Sarajevo or parts of Sarajevo not populated by predominantly -- by Serbs should be taken. Their goal was to defend their villages, houses, properties, and the population that lived there. The supreme commander's order of June 1992 stated that all-out defence should be launched from the existing surrounding defence lines. His unit took his -- this order seriously since they were aware of the fact that should their defence lines be penetrated anywhere in the area surrounding Sarajevo, large forces would be released from the city and this advantage would seal the fate of the war. Thus, the forces of the 1st Corps of BH army desperately tried to break out of the city. They launched offensives in 1992, March 1993, and ones that hit Miladin Trifunovic's unit harder, April and June 1995. Serb military and civilian authorities surrendered the Sarajevo airport so that humanitarian aid could be provided through it. UNPROFOR convoys frequently passed through his zone of defence transporting humanitarian aid for the population in Sarajevo. They did not disrupt these convoys in their mission, although it became obvious later on that military equipment for the needs of the BH army had been brought to Sarajevo under the guise of humanitarian aid. Every soldier and officer in his unit was informed of the orders issued by the superior military and civilian authorities, commanding strict adherence to the provisions of the international law of war prohibiting the opening of fire against civilians and civilian facilities. In any case, in the area facing his unit's line of defence there were no civilian targets that could have been affected. His unit never launched such bombs, at least while he was its commander. Regarding incident G-17 [sic] when a bomb landed in Dositejeva Street 4a on 16th of June, 1995, Miladin Trifunovic states with full responsibility such bombs were never launched either from the Pretis factory or from any other locations within the brigade's zone of defence. G-14, maybe I was -- pronounced G-17. G-14 incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There are a few brief questions that I would like to put to you, Mr. Trifunovic. Were you ever arrested by the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber when this took place and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of December, 1992, because strong Green Beret forces attacked Zuc, and at that point in time, we were not able to drive them back and they drove us back to the hill 830, which was the extreme limit after which they could have entered the inhabited part of Vogosca. The fighting continued from the 5th of December up until the time I went to prison, and after that too. Fortunately, we managed to hold them there and they didn't pass through that last hill where we were struggling all the time. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you placed in detention?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I spent three days in Ilijas and three days and three nights in the so-called Planja Kuca prison in Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were only Serbs detained in that house or were there any detainees from other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were members of other ethnic groups in that house and we were there too, me and my four assistants and all the leadership of the Rajlovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many Serbs were there and how many other people were there and from which ethnic groups, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what the number is. I know that there were four of us. There was 17 Serbs from Rajlovac, that makes 21; as for the number of Muslim detainees, I don't know what that number is, nor do I know the number of Croat detainees. All I know is they were in the room adjacent to the one that we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These Muslims and Croats, were they prisoners of war or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were all prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any Muslim and Croat women and children in that detention centre?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many floors did that house have?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Three floors and there was the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the rooms in which you were detained, you and the other detainees, were they aired? Did you have enough air?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the rooms were large ones. They had large windows. There was a lot of light. There was everything that a house needs or that such rooms need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that it was in December, did you have any heating?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have toilets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have showers? Were you able to wash yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you and the other detainees -- well, was -- were any differences made, any distinctions made, between you and the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of food did you have? Did you have a kitchen that you could use and how did you prepare food?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We prepared food in the Pretis factory canteen for the entire army, and that food would be distributed to the positions and the food would be brought in certain containers and distributed to the soldiers and me as a detainee at the time. It would also be distributed to the other prisoners who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: Was there a kitchen in that house? Was that a residential house? What kind of a house was that? What kind of a building?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was a newly built residential house. There was a room where -- for a kitchen and there was a dining room or a sitting room, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you -- did the detainees suffer physical ill treatment in Planjina Kula while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not observe any such thing while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And a few questions about something that you mentioned. You said that the Serbian municipality of Vogosca had been set up. Did you control the entire municipality of Vogosca or actually did the Muslim municipality of Vogosca exist?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not control the entire municipality of Vogosca. At the very beginning, the political leaderships of both the Serbian people and the Muslim people had agreed and created two Muslims effectively. The Muslim side was on one side and we were on the other side, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you didn't ask the witness why he was arrested, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did. Because they lost Zuc, they could not maintain the control of Zuc on the 15th of December. I asked him and that's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because the Green Berets had mounted an attack on Zuc and they lost it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So was that the reason for your detention, Mr. Trifunovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what was mentioned in my indictment. That's one of the counts in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were indicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was detained because I had lost a part of the terrain on Zuc. As the most responsible person in the brigade, I was responsible for that as well. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether you were indicted? Did you have a trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you were in detention for six days; that's it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not on trial. There was no indictment. I just heard the explanation as to why I had been detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As the Serbian territorial guard, later on the Serbian army, did you control a predominantly Muslim settlement with a predominantly Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: By and large, no. The lines were established very early on. As soon as guards were mounted, the lines were also established to indicate what sector belonged to what people, and that's how things persisted until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned in your statement that convoys passed through. From which direction did they arrive before -- from before they reached your area of responsibility and what was your attitude towards them? I don't mean you personally but of our army?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The convoys passed from Sarajevo towards Zenica and the other way around. I don't know of any incidents. They were never stopped or ill-treated. Their passage was always unobstructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were the orders and instructions from the superior commands and the civilian authorities with regard to those convoys?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Every order that we received in that respect was putting a strict ban on ill-treating Red Cross convoy staff or stopping them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. At this point in time I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar [sic], may I have 65 ter 1D12001 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, as this map comes up on the screen you will see that it was the map that -- which has a red line on it showing the Vogosca Brigade's line of defence. That was apparently marked by you. Do you recognise that map?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Can this be zoomed in a little? Can this be made more visible?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we zoom in to where the red line is, please, in the middle of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, is that the map that -- where you drew the red line on?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, do you recall marking a map with a red line of your line of defence when you spoke with the Defence when you provided your statement? Is that the --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- map --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. With the usher's help, can you please draw on this map your zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can bring the map down so that the red line is towards the bottom of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mark it with the marker pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we zoom in, please, bring the map down and zoom in on the red line. You need to go out a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to zoom out --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We need to zoom out again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The resolution of this map is very poor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, we may come back to that. Can you please describe what your zone of responsibility was. What was the depth of your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: My zone of responsibility, the zone of responsibility of my brigade, was on Zuc hill. The Gola Brdo elevation across the trigger point 830, across one part of Ugljesici, it passed through -- or across the Vogosca-Sarajevo road. Partly it went along the Pretis perimeter, along the upper Hotonj towards Poljine, where it linked up with the Kosevo Brigade. When it comes to that line of responsibility in the direction of Sarajevo, that is, when it comes to the line of defence in depth of our territory behind our lines which faced Breza, it extended from Donja Vogosca. It went across Ravno Navosce and descended to the Sarajevo-Semizovac-Olovo road. And it went all the way to Gora and it inter -- crossed the river where it came down to Motka, the Ubare settlement which is up there.
