That was the depth of my territory, i.e., the depth of my zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you had support forces. What were your support forces?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: My support forces consisted of artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First of all, we'll deal with the infantry. You had five battalions, the Semizovac Battalion, Blagovac, Hotonj, Vogosca, and Krivoglavci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So what was the number of infantrymen?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the number varied from 1500 to 1800 and that would be a total comprising the logistics support and everything that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was the military post number for your brigade VP7003?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned artillery. What artillery did the brigade have? In your statement you say -- you mention 88-millimetre [sic] and 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 80- and 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many 88-millimetre -- 82-millimetre [sic] mortars did you have?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Every battalion had approximately two such weapons, ten all together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: While I was a member of the command, four in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were these artillery positioned?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: On Blagovac hill and in Krivoglavci. I'm talking about 120-millimetre heavy mortars, whereas the smaller-calibre mortars were deployed in the sectors of their respective battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the targets if we are talking generally and I want to know about Sarajevo in particular. So, first of all, in relation to the 88-millimetre -- 82-millimetre mortars, what were their targets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We were far from Sarajevo. We did not target Sarajevo from our 82-millimetre mortars. There were no targets for us there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the targets of the 82-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Exclusively military targets which appeared on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them appeared on Zuc hill, and the rest depended on where the incoming fire came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What about 120-millimetre targets -- mortars, where were their targets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Ninety per cent were aimed towards Zuc hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And where were the other 10 per cent aimed?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: A mortar is a mobile weapon. It does not stay put and aims at just one target. 120-millimetre mortars were aimed towards Zuc and we often opened -- we were all -- very often targeted but by their artillery below Hum hill and when that happened we defended ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, you said that 90 per cent were aimed towards Zuc hill and 10 per cent perhaps towards Hum, but then you also said that they were --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- mobile. So where did you -- where were they located when they were mobile? Where did you take them?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, a mortar is not mobile. Its direction, the direction of its target, can be changed. It can aim for Zuc hill from the same place; it doesn't have to be moved. Just the barrel is moved. New elements are calculated, and when that happens, the mortar may be aimed at Hum hill, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I understand. Besides the 82-millimetre and 122-millimetre mortars, what other artillery did you have available?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We had a 105-millimetre howitzer and a 122-millimetre howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just need to go back to the military post number. I think I said VP 7003. I meant to say -- and you agreed with me, I think. Isn't it VP 7033?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your number, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Earlier, a few minutes ago I said that the military post number for your brigade was VP 7003 and you agreed with me, but it's, in fact, VP 7033, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd now like to look at a few documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 01224A on the screen, please. If we could go to page 8 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it been released, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will just check, Your Honour. It's been done now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All it says is it equals to D1202 -- we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I really am struggling with numbers this morning. It's 12204. My apologies. If we can go to page 8. I'm sorry, in mine it's page 8 -- but if we can go to -- it's a very short document, it's only four pages. If we can flip through to the one dated the 23rd of September, please. If we can go back a previous page. And again. To the 23rd of September. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, you see there that there is a request for pieces of -- 20 pieces of 120-millimetre LTF mortar shells and 30 pieces of 105-millimetre howitzer shells. And you mentioned a moment ago the 105-millimetres. Whereabouts were they positioned and what were their targets?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is not a request issued by my brigade. This is a request by the Igman Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Actually it's the Hadzici Brigade. I'm looking for the Vogosca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hadzici Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this 12204A?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Trifunovic, can you tell me where your 105-millimetre howitzer shells were positioned and what their targets were?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Both 105- and 120-millimetre howitzers were on a hilltop above Blagovac and their targets were the same as our mortar targets. Very often we did not have enough shells either for the mortars or for the howitzers and that's why we overcame that difficulty. We had to defend ourselves and when we did that we used either or.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, let's be clear with the document. The document we saw earlier on was a -- on page 6 of 65 ter 12204 and what we see now is 12204A.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But dated --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- 23rd of September. When I called up the number originally I said the wrong exhibit number and I said it with an A, but when it was called up again the exhibit without the A came up so the big document, in fact, came up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the number with A shows the date of 21st --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- does it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There's eight pages in the range. The page I wanted was on page 7 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We have it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, we can see there the document in front of us is the 23rd of September where you have requested to be provided with 32 pieces of 122-millimetre TFG SP shell. Is that a self-propelled shell?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what kind of weapon you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You see here the first one, 122-millimetre TFG SP shell. Does the "SP" stand for self-propelled?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is a round. No, a howitzer is located in one position. It cannot be self-propelled and it's not easily movable, it's not easily mobile, and its rounds were manufactured by the Pretis factory. It is fired in a regular fashion. It is certainly not self-propelled. It cannot be self-propelled. This "SP" stands for the markings of the factory. I'm not an artillery guy. I don't know much about this, but I know that this cannot be self-propelled. I know that the rounds were produced by the Pretis factory and I really don't know what else to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell me where -- you said that they were quite -- they're not easily movable. Where were these -- first of all, how many of these mortars did your brigade have, 122-millimetres howitzers?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning I said that we had one howitzer while I was commander. It was a 120-millimetre howitzer and we had a 105-millimetre howitzer as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Right. But we can see here that you've just ordered 32 shells for 122-millimetre howitzer. So your brigade must have had at least one. So my question is: How many did your brigade have?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I was clear. In 1992 there was just one howitzer of that calibre and another one, one 105-millimetre howitzer. That's what my brigade had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So why in your statement did you say that you only had -- your brigade only had 82-millimetre and 105 -- 120-millimetre mortars, when we can see here that - and you've just said - that you had 122-millimetre howitzer and 105-millimetre howitzer?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 1 of this document -- oh, sorry, not page 1, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, we see here the very next -- or two days later, three days later, you're requesting another 80 pieces of 105-millimetre TGF shell, 80 pieces of 120-millimetres, and 21 pieces of 122-millimetres. And if we can go to page 6, it shows that you got exactly what you asked for. And it was received by Aleksa Jokic, is that right, at the Blagojevic [sic] Brigade -- it states "brigade," but in fact Blagojevic was a battalion, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Blagojevic Battalion, yes. But as I said, the artillery was located in the area of responsibility of the Blagojevic Battalion on the hill, and that is why it was delivered to them, up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can just quickly go to page 8 of this document - I meant to do it a moment ago -- page 9, I'm sorry -- oh, 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, that shows -- that's going back to -- the document we just looked at on the 23rd of September, and that shows that again you got exactly what you asked for on the 23rd of September, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 3 in e-court, and this is just another request on the 24th of September for a hundred pieces of 122-millimetre mortars. And if we go to the next page, page 4, it shows that that was dispatched on that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we go to page 1, and this is dated the 21st of September, from the 3rd Hotonj Battalion, and that's within the Vogosca Brigade, is it not, requesting a hundred pieces of 122-millimetre [sic] mortar shells because they've reached a critical minimum "because we have participated in operations to mop-up Zuc." You agreed with me earlier that Hotonj Battalion was in the Vogosca Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But if you'd mopped up Zuc on the 21st of September, which this document says, what was the need in the four-day period between the 23rd and the 26th of September for requesting 513 pieces of howitzer shells and mortar shells for two battalions?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean, "mopped-up Zuc." We didn't mop-up Zuc throughout the war time-period. Zuc is a plateau. It's a very wide area and there was fighting there all the time throughout the war. And from Sarajevo there were forceful forces from the Muslim army coming in our direction; they were stronger than our forces. All we had was the protection that these sort of artillery pieces provided us with. They drove us back to trig point 830 in spite of that, as I said at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, they're not my words, they're your battalion's words, "mopping-up." But again, you still haven't answered the question. Where were your 122-millimetre howitzers positioned?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, do we understand each other or not? I said that we had in 1992, while I was the brigade commander, one 120-millimetre howitzer on a hill, on Blagovac, and we used that howitzer from that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you haven't told me what the targets were for that howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said. The exclusive targets were the Zuc plateau; that was the exclusive target. I said that a while ago and I'll repeat that. The Vogosca Brigade focused on the Zuc plateau practically throughout the war-time period.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. You're saying that you don't have any targets in Sarajevo proper; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You agree that 122-millimetre howitzer is a large, sophisticated, expensive weapon; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it has a maximum range of up to 15 kilometres, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's quite good for blowing up buildings, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. This artillery piece can be used to attack trenches, fortified bunkers, and so on and so forth. It can't destroy a building. Perhaps it can fire on a building, but as for blowing it up, that's out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How far is Vogosca from the city?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: About 15 kilometres. It depends where you measure the distance from, from which part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: To the centre.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps up to 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Twenty kilometres from Vogosca to the centre of Sarajevo? Isn't it more 5 to 7?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P00836 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is okay, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I can just deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- with this document and then we can take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, you see here this is an order from Dragomir Milosevic dated the 15th of July, 1993, and it's sent to all units in brigade regiments and specifically makes mention of the Vogosca Tactical Group. And it says: "All units are forbidden to fire on Sarajevo proper, unless defending VRS positions." So my question is: Why would there be a need to send this order to the Vogosca Brigade if it wasn't either firing on Sarajevo proper or if it didn't have the capacity to do so?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this order is from 1993. I wasn't a commander at the time. But a larger army formation such as a corps, when it sends an order, if it's of a general nature, it sends that order to all the units within its corps. This only concerns prohibition on using artillery ammunition to fire on the town. It includes those who can act in such a way and those who can't. So these things are sent out to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned the date was in 1993, when you were -- when you weren't the commander of the Vogosca Brigade. But you were still within the Vogosca Brigade because you were commander of the Blagojevic Battalion, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the commander of the Blagovac Battalion, but when I take a different, lower position, I don't receive such orders from the corps, I receive them from the brigade commander, and this was probably sent to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 12.33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I ask for Exhibit -- 65 ter 12204A to be admitted, please. That was the list of four pages within the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we would have no objection to those pages which were used during the examination being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but I was wondering whether we saw only four pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I went to the first exhibit number that I called out and then I realised that it wasn't the correct exhibit and we went to the correct exhibit. So that's the document that I seek to tender. But I will be going back to that other bigger document shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, we'll admit those pages we've dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5995, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, you said in your statement that neither your brigade, i.e., the Vogosca Brigade, nor any of the neighbouring ones ever carried out any offensive operations. We'll leave aside your neighbouring brigades, but that's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter number 24072.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I mean that you actually ordered and carried out offensive activities; do you agree? Mr. Trifunovic, can you just answer the question that I put to you before you look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you ordered and carried out offensive activities, contrary to what you state in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer the question before reading this to see what it's about. We were engaged in offensive --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- action on the hill of Zuc exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- I'll interrupt you there, Mr. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the Registrar can take the document off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's a simple question. Do you agree that you participated in and, in fact, ordered offensive operations, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Partially, yes, but it depends on the area concerned. If we're talking about the area of Zuc, then yes. In certain situations it was necessary to improve the position. If we came under sniper fire, so then yes. But as for attacking the depth of Sarajevo and so on and so forth, in that case my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But -- so why did you put in your statement that neither you or the other neighbouring brigades ever carried out any offensive activities, when you've just said that you did?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Offensive operations on the plateau of Zuc. This isn't considered as offensive action because the Zuc plateau was inhabited exclusively by Serbs, and all the combatants up there, most of them, wanted to go to their homes to approach their graves. That's the problem. So I don't consider that to be offensive action. This is no more than a matter of taking back territory that we lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, that's your -- one interpretation, Mr. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have the document back on the screen, 65 ter 24072.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is dated the 6th of October, 1992, and it's an order for attack which is actually signed on your behalf as commander of the Vogosca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2 and page 3 in the B/C/S -- and page 3 in the English, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who signed this order on your behalf? Is this Mr. Kenic your deputy of the -- who was deputy of the Vogosca Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we go back to page 1, this is about an attack on Orlic, is it not? And the attack is scheduled for the 7th of October. Isn't this an order for an attack, an offensive action?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The hill of Orlic, trig point 877, is in the wider area of the Zuc plateau. It dominates all the other trig points that we have already mentioned in the area of Zuc. The Orlic hill and below consisted of Serbian territory. Up until the 8th of June, 1992, that territory was under the control of the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska. But on the 8th of June, when the Muslim forces launched an attack, they drove us back from trig point 877 as far as trig point 850. So as I have said, this is no more than a matter of taking back territory that we had previously lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, but it's an offensive action, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not an offensive operation. If you try to return your territory, to get back to your homes, this is what people strove for. The houses of all these people were in the vicinity of trig point 877, near the Orlic hill and below. And the wider area of that plateau isn't densely inhabited.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I have to express concern about this debate or issue of whether certain operation was of defensive nature or offensive nature. It leads us nowhere. Bear that in mind -- both parties should bear that in mind. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5996, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 24166 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, we can see here this is a report dated the 13th of October, 1992. It's from the Vogosca Brigade command, which is you, to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps OG 1, and you're reporting on the conditions and combat operations in the zone of responsibility for the brigade. It says here: "In the following period we are planning the take-over of the Zuc line ..." and mentions the trig points and cleansing of the villages Ugorsko, Menjak and Barica. Who lived in those villages, Ugorsko, Menjak, and Barica?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Ugorsko, Menjak, and Barica were inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5997, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we just quickly go back to exhibit -- 65 ter number 12204.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, this is quite a number of documents, individual documents, requests from and dispatches to battalions within the Vogosca Operative Group, that is, Vogosca, Rajlovac, Ilijas, and there's also dispatches from Hadzici, Ilidza, Lukavac, Blazuj, and Nedzarici. I'm interested in taking you to one in relation to your brigade and that's on page 7 -- page 3. It's for the 17th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can we have the same page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We see here this is a huge variety -- in fact, ten different types of weapons and almost 2.000 artillery weapons dispatched to Aco Jokic from your brigade. And it includes 155-millimetre guns M1 howitzer, 105-millimetre howitzer M56, 76-millimetre mountain gun B1, 76-millimetre gun ZiS, and 122-millimetre howitzer Gvozdika. What did you need, on the 17th of October, almost 2.000 artillery weapons for? Is this in relation to the planned take-over of the Zuc line that we saw back in Exhibit P5997?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, we are talking of shells, not the weapons themselves; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the need for almost 2.000 artillery weapons [sic] on the 17th of October? And I said was this in relation to the planning that we saw in Exhibit P5997 a moment ago in relation to the planning of the take-over of Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The ammunition that we needed -- in the territory of Vogosca there was the Vogosca Tactical Group which was composed of three brigades: The Kosevo Brigade, the Vogosca Brigade, and the Rajlovac Brigade. What was issued was issued through the Vogosca Brigade in order to be distributed among all the other brigades. The tactical brigade Vogosca had been established and deployed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can quickly go to page 2, it shows on the 22nd of October again five different types of weapons and over a hundred pieces dispatched to the Vogosca Brigade. And if we go to page 1 -- sorry, that was on the 22nd of October. And if we go to page 1 deals with the 23rd of October, 1992, six different types of weapons and 450 pieces dispatched. Do you see that there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But I have told you that Vogosca was the centre from which things were distributed amongst the other brigades, the Kosevo Brigade and the Rajlovac Brigade which were issued with weapons, equipment, ammunition, from the depot. And that quantity was issued for all the three brigades, i.e., for the entire tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement, and this is -- you note that the Muslims had many more soldiers than the Serbs. But it's a fact, isn't it, that the VRS - and in this case the SRK - had superior weaponry to the opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must assist with the interpretation. Madam Sutherland used the word "soldiers" which was interpreted as "troops" -- or rather, Madam Sutherland said "weapons" and it was interpreted as "troops." The transcript reads well and it is a good reflection of what Madam Sutherland said, but the Serbian interpretation was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you understand the question, Mr. Trifunovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the question but I'm waiting to see what's next. When it comes to the manpower and the numerical strength, i.e., armed and equipped soldiers, their strength was three or four times superior to ours. There is a report from a brigade commander who was on the opposition side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My question was -- I noted that you said that there were -- that the Muslims had more soldiers than the Serbs, but it's a fact, isn't it, that the VRS had the superior weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know what they had. I know what we had. I really can't say what they had. I wasn't there. Luckily enough, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just go back to -- you asked me a question a moment ago: "Ms. Sutherland, are we talking of shells not the weapons themselves; correct?" And I said: "Yes, artillery weapons." In fact I misspoke and I did mean shells. You were right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm a bit confused. You said what Ms. Sutherland stated was correct. What did you mean? You agree that Serbs had superior weaponry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if they had superior weaponry. It's just my estimate. They may have had superior weaponry. I don't know. I don't know what they had. I only know what we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, you know what they had in relation -- I'll move on. I want to move on to another topic now. You completed officers school in 1976, didn't you, and you were discharged with the rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the officers school in Bileca and I obtained the rank of second lieutenant. As a member of the reserve that existed in the former Yugoslavia, I was promoted all the way to the rank of a captain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, before I forget, may I tender the pages of exhibit 12204 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We dealt with two pages or three pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, as an officer, a captain, and a commanding officer at the brigade level you're familiar with the regulations relating to the use of detained persons, either civilians or prisoners of war in relation to work, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, exhibit number shall be Exhibit P5998. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to show you a series of documents now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 24081 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 18th of October, 1992, signed by you, for 30 detainees to be used on Zuc on the 19th of October for construction work. And there's a reference in the predicate paragraph to item 10 of the Instruction on the Treatment of Prisoners. That's number 21-26/92 of the 13th of June, 1992. I also see that you copied the prison warden and the War Commission. What type of construction work did the detainees perform when they were taken to Zuc?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They mostly fortified the lines, things like that, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What do you mean by "fortifying the lines"? Can you just explain that in layman terms.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: So far I've stated that there was ongoing combat on Zuc hill. Throughout the war there was always combat going on. We moved the line to and fro all the time. We did not have the time to fortify our lines. That's why we used our own forces and additional forces in order to fortify those lines because we did not have either the time or the opportunity to do that properly, given the activities and the incoming fire from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can that document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5999, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P02385.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 17th of September, 1992, number 11 of 84 [sic] and it's signed by you as commander of the Vogosca command. And you request 50 prisoners for work in the field on the 18th of September, 1992. What type of work did detainees usually perform in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is again on Zuc hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I just have a moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, the Court has heard evidence before it from Witness Eset Muracevic in relation to this particular request that 50 men were taken from Planjo's house and used as human shields to move the front line and that some were killed and a number wounded, and that the wounded told the other detainees when they returned that they were used as human shields.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I refer the Trial Chamber and the accused to Exhibit P02361, page 26, item number 34 and paragraphs 69 to 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which was admitted pursuant to 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 92 ter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you spell the witness name again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: M-u-r-a-c-e-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Eset Muracevic. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May that document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said Eset, instead of Esad. Yes, this will be -- that's already in evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Yes. Can I have Exhibit P01144, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I don't think the witness was given the benefit to answer any question concerning this document. Can we hear from the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's correct --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He did. I asked him -- I said what type of work did detainees usually perform in the field and he said this was at Zuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Was that the last question, Ms. Sutherland, you asked?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. He said: "This is again on Zuc hill." So I was taking that he was meaning fortified positions. But we can ask the witness to confirm that the work on Zuc was again as he had previously said, fortifying the positions and moving the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I said fortifying the positions and accessing the positions. Fortifying the accesses to those positions which led to Zuc hill where we were chased away to a different trig point. We did not have enough trenches or at least -- or rather, we did not have any trenches at all through which we could access the hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit P01144, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Excellencies, what about the comment proffered about Muracevic? No questions were asked. The witness didn't say anything about people being taken away as human shields. It appeared to be nothing less than testimony on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you can put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The witness -- the witness said that they were taken to Zuc, that they were used for fortifying and moving the front line. I was simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you reminded of some content of Witness Muracevic and you didn't put that to the witness. I think it's fair to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, would you like to comment on Mr. Muracevic's evidence that I just summarised for you in relation to that request for 50 men?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Muracevic said, but I claim with full responsibility that they were never used for that purpose, the purpose that he mentioned. Both we and ourselves [as interpreted] were used for one and only purpose and that was improving access trenches to the line, fortifying --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Both we and ourselves." Both them and ourselves. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are overlapping again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both them and ourselves were used and they were never used without us and they were only used for improving accesses to the lines and for fortifying the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and that's exactly what you said on page 68 when I said: "What do you mean by fortifying the lines? Can you explain it in layman terms?" You said: "We moved the line to and fro all the time. We did not have the time to fortify our lines. That's why we used our own forces and additional forces ..." - and by "additional forces," do you mean the detainees from Planjo's house? - "in order to fortify the lines because we did not have either the time nor the opportunity to do that properly, given the activities and incoming fire from Sarajevo." So, first of all, when you said back on page 68 "additional forces," you were referring to the document we had just been discussing, the detainees from Planjo's, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I said that we together with them, we took them with us. And let me explain, on that day, the 17th or the 18th, I was wounded before that even started. So we could not use them as the living shields because on that day we had 11 casualties among our soldiers, 11 dead. As soon as we started fortifying the line, the Muslim forces must have noticed us --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could stop you there. If I could stop you there, we'll get to when you were injured in a little while, Mr. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that that satisfies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we can move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now if we can look at P01144. This is on the screen now. It's dated the 19th of September, 1992. It's a bulletin for the 18th of September, 1992, for reporting on the deaths and wounding of detainees who were taken to Zuc hill. The report makes a specific reference to your request 11/84. And this report, is it signed by Branko Vlaco's deputy, Nebojsa Spiric.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So in relation to work performed in the field, this Trial Chamber's also heard evidence before it in relation to Witness Bego Selimovic, whose relative is listed in P01144, who was used as a human shield on the 18th of September, when he died. And on the 19th or the 20th of September, 1992, the witness was selected to go to Zuc to look for his body. And when he was there, he had to carry with another detainee the body of a dead man up to the command while being beaten with a piece of wood. And he was later then made to carry ammunition and water.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I refer the Trial Chamber and the accused to Exhibit P0046, paragraph numbers 28 and 29, but also generally through paragraphs 26 to 38, and also Exhibit P00045.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you have any comment to make in relation to that summary of evidence, Mr. Trifunovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we deal with one by one. Can you confirm with this document first and then go on with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This document is a bulletin, is it not, setting out who were killed and who were wounded the day that they were taken to Zuc pursuant to your request; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat, on that day, on the 18th of September, as soon as we --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, I'll stop --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- arrived on Zuc --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- you there. My question was simply: Can you confirm what this document is about, as I just put to you, that it's a document, a bulletin, by the -- signed on behalf of the warden of the prison setting out who was killed and who was wounded in relation to a request by you to take them to Zuc for work in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: You do not allow me to express myself. As soon as we got on Zuc on the 18th of September, I was wounded and taken away --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Stop you there --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- to the hospital and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, I will stop you there. My question was simply: Do you agree that that's what the document says? You've already said the circumstances about your wounding; I'm not interested in that for the moment. Is what I put to you what the document states?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we can read what is there. But, Mr. Trifunovic, irrespective of how many Serb soldiers were wounded or killed, do you confirm that four prisoners were killed and seven prisoners were wounded due to the field work in Zuc? Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that people did get killed, but I don't know how many, before -- because I had been taken to hospital. So I wouldn't know how many died, how many were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you see this report. You would not question the veracity of this document, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether it is true or not. I wasn't there. I can't tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, I would seek to have the document admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, the Trial Chamber has also heard evidence before it in relation -- has evidence before it in relation to Witness Mustafa Fazlic who was -- describes being used as a human shield on the 17th or the 18th of September when 50 detainees were taken to Zuc. He describes being made to walk with 20 of the men in a long line in front of the soldiers at the time they started shelling the position they were about to attack. That is, the Serbs. They had to look for mines in front of them while the soldiers were shooting from behind the detainees' backs. His brother, who was next to him, was shot. He was also made to go and get ammunition. And he mentions the names of two of the persons who are listed in the bulletin we just saw, P01144.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I refer the Trial Chamber and the accused to P00042, pages 4 to 6. Again, do you have any comment to make on the summary I just read? Is this the type of work that you were having the detainees do on Zuc?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I can claim with full responsibility that no one used them for such purposes, but only in order to fortify the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, back on, I think, page 68, that you used them to move the lines. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I have exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. We didn't. That's not what was said. What was said is that we were continually moving the line back. The Muslim forces were driving us back and, as a result, we had to withdraw. We weren't moving the line forward. There's a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit P2387, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, this is dated the 22nd of September, 1992. It's a bulletin for the 21st of September, 1992, from prison warden Brano Vlaco -- Branko Vlaco reporting on there being eight detainees wounded and two detainees killed at Zuc, making specific reference to your request dated 11/74 of the 17th of September, 1992. And again it's signed by his deputy, Nebojsa Spiric. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence that detainees that were taken out were forced to carry out various jobs mainly on the front lines, including the digging of trenches, communication trenches, and other fortification features as well as carrying of ammunition and heavy weaponry. And that such jobs carried out on the front lines actually took part along the lines of separation between the Serbian army and the Bosnian army where the majority of detainees were exposed to fire from both sides. And this is Mr. Muracevic's testimony at transcript pages 12653 to 12654. Do you have any comment to make on the summary of evidence that I've just read?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was no need for them to dig in front of our front line. They were never alone without us nor did they ever go in front of us in order to dig. Why? We weren't defending there, so we were all there together, we were working, the VRS was with them, the Army of Republika Srpska. So there was never a need to use them for such purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So when the Bosnian Serb army were walking along, where were the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? When they were walking along? Where? That is a plateau, a hill. You can't walk around. You have to stay underground. You can't just walk around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 24082 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 22nd of September, 1992, from you to the prison to provide 30 prisoners for, again, construction work at the Zuc location. And again you reference Article 10 of the Instruction on the Treatment of Prisoners. And you've copied it to the War Commission. And this order states that it comes into effect on the 26th of September, 1992, and remains in effect for as long as necessary. So, again, you agree that this is an order for more construction work for an indefinite period, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not for an indefinite period. This was according to the needs because action was daily. So the issue on that day was whether we would lose or not, whether the Muslims would enter Vogosca or not. So we asked everyone who could, even women, to go up there to fortify the lines and to prevent the Muslims from penetrating the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which women are you talking about? Where from?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Women of Serbian ethnicity who were among the ranks of the troops, who were working in the canteens, who were from logistics sector and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Is it Exhibit 6000? Yes. Exhibit P6000. Have we seen that document referred to in this document, i.e., Instruction on the Treatment of Prisoners --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- issued by the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- be showing you in just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's an exhibit. Okay if we can quickly look at P2338 [sic]. This is dated the 24th of -- 2388. It's a document dated the 24th of September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It says here that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at the time I wasn't there. I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's just concerning the killing of two detainees because they were hit by fire while carrying out works at the Zuc hill. And you've actually made your comment about that document now. But are you aware that detainees were hit by fire when they were taken for work on Zuc?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th -- no, I don't believe I was aware of that. I was in the hospital from the 18th. I wasn't there during those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Generally are you aware that detainees were hit by fire while carrying out works at Zuc?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm now telling you that I wasn't aware of the fact because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Trifunovic, I was going to deal with it a little later but I'll deal with it now. You said you were injured on the 18th of September, 1992. In fact, apart --

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- from the fact that it says in the English translation of your statement that it's the 18th of December, we'll leave that aside because it's a translation. But in another document, a statement that you gave to the Serbian authorities when you were arrested at the end of December, you said that you were arrested on the 18th of October, 1992. So which is it? Is it September or is it October? Would you like to see that statement, the other statement?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was placed in detention on the 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I'm not concerned about when you were placed in detention. I'm -- oh, sorry, I misspoke. When you were wounded, not when you were arrested. I'm sorry. Is it September or October?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 18th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So why would you tell the Serbian authorities in a statement that you gave in December when you were arrested that you were wounded on the 18th of October?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a typing error, but this is certainly referred to in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get back to where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have the last two documents in this series and that's P02383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you, both parties, that we need to rise 1.45 sharp, considering the next hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I won't be completed by 1.45, but I understood that that's when we were finishing for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that this witness should be brought back --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in two weeks' time --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I had estimated two and a half hours for cross-examination and I didn't start my cross-examination until around 11.30 today. So I still have roughly 45 minutes left by the end of -- at the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, we can see here this is dated the 12th of September, 1992. It's a Semizovac Battalion request number 24 of 92, signed by Lieutenant Zoran Torbica for Commander Colakovic, for prisoners to work on the front lines and they're needed for 11 days from the 13th to the 24th of September, 1992, because they want the men to dig trenches on the front line of the 3rd Company Ravno. I will show you the next document and then I will ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P02392, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this is dated the 25th of November, 1992, again Semizovac Battalion, request number 104/92 for prisoners to work on the front lines "... in order to move the front line. We need the prisoners on the 26th of November ..." So they're just stating it right up front that they want to use the prisoners in order to move the front line. The Semizovac barracks was a battalion under your command, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: That was in the area of responsibility of our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the document says they're in order to move the front line and your position on that's not changing, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, moving the front line -- well, it concerned fortification, improving positions at the front line. How were they to move the front line? With what? We would be improving the positions and fortifying the positions at that front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, you -- the use of detainees to carry out work such as digging trenches, fortifying, carrying ammunition and material and being used to move the front line, not only did it violate basic provisions of the Geneva Conventions requiring the humane treatment of prisoners of war and civilians, it also violates the prohibition in the conventions of using either prisoners of war or civilians in work that is directly related to military activities, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We have an order from the Ministry of Defence at the time according to which it is possible to make use of them provided they are not exposed to danger. And in our opinion, they were never exposed to danger since we were all there together. In such case, we were all in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were never exposed to danger, then how were people killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that they weren't there alone. We were there together, so we were all exposed. They were there when that work was being carried out, they were there together with our troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So that's all right, then. If they're there with your troops, then that's okay, to take detainees to work in combat areas; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm only referring to the ministerial order that was compiled by the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I have Exhibit P01134, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this the Instruction on the Treatment of Prisoners that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2 in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that what you were talking about by the minister of defence, Mr. Subotic, issuing these instructions on the treatment of prisoners? Mr. Trifunovic, is that what you were talking about, this document?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see this very well, but this is probably the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go back to page 1 of the English and B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could show the Serbian version, 1D298, it's more legible. The English one can remain. 1D298 could perhaps be shown, as it is more legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mind, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Not at all. Now if we can zoom in on paragraph 10. Unfortunately, in the B/C/S, paragraph 10 goes over two pages, but so -- if we just rid of the English for the moment so that we can let the witness read the entirety of paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And let me know when you've read that provision.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 10, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can reduce the B/C/S and bring the English back, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So we can see, Mr. Trifunovic, that Article 10, the one that you've been quoting in your documents when you request prisoners from Planjo's is: "Besides work connected with the cleaning and maintenance of the camp, captured persons may be put to work in agriculture, industry, mining, handicrafts, traffic, trade, and other areas which are not directly related to war operations." So how do you reconcile taking someone to a combat zone with this order with these instructions? Would you like me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead then, repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So I read Article 10. Would you like me to read the contents of Article 10 again? I don't think I need to do that. My question was after I read the article: How do you reconcile taking someone to a combat zone with this -- with these instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says they can't be used for fortifying camps. These aren't camps. These are lines, trenches for defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. The article says: "... which are not directly related to war operations."

utterances.speaker: MILADIN TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that they are not directly related to war operations if we are working together at fortifying the positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, shall we stop here and discuss how to proceed from herein terms of scheduling. Mr. Trifunovic, we'll have to adjourn very soon for today and we are going to have a long break after this and resume only on -- in the week after, i.e., Tuesday, 27th of November. So I apologise for your inconvenience, but I have to ask whether there would be no problem on your part to return to The Hague to complete your evidence, Mr. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate your kind understanding. Two or three minutes. Is there any matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- can the witness be instructed not to discuss his evidence with anyone, including the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't have any further question for today?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, we'll adjourn now, but I'd like to advise you about the rule and practice at the Tribunal which is that the witness is not supposed to discuss about his testimony with anybody else while or until he completes his evidence. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of November, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
